name: Queen's Park 1872–89
scopeNote: Queen's Park FC (Glasgow) in the combination era, 1872 to 1889. Start: the FA Cup semi-final with the Wanderers at Kennington Oval, 1872-03-05 (Wikipedia, 1871-72 FA Cup; Robinson's 1920 club history dates it 4 March), the first dated competitive match of the era; the club had played since 1867. The 1872-11-30 Scotland v England international is counted because all eleven Scotland players were Queen's Park players and the team was picked by the Queen's Park captain. End: partial date, year 1889, a convention kept from the earlier decision to match the combination-game ideology's end (Preston North End's 1888-89 double); the club played on as an amateur club. No head coach existed: the team was run by an elected captain with 'absolute' power until 29 April 1880, then by a match committee, so managers[] is empty by design. Style name: 'combination', the period term. Alcock (Football Annual 1878, quoted in Wilson et al. 2025) credits 'the combination of dribbling and passing' for the Queen's Park eleven; a 1875 match reporter calls its play 'much the more scientific, all of their forwards relying upon their skill in dribbling'. The popular label 'Queen's Park invented the passing game' is not supported: Wilson et al. (2025) find passing in Sheffield in the 1860s and conclude passing was 'effectively deployed, but not necessarily invented in Scotland'; the Scots Football Historians Group places the Scottish passing game in the Vale of Leven/Renton.
openQuestions: Start date: Wikipedia (1871-72 FA Cup) and the old file give 1872-03-05 for the Wanderers semi-final; Robinson's club history (ch. IX) gives 4 March 1872. The 1872-03-05 start was kept as decided; confirm it.
End of the era (1889) is a convention, not a club event; the 1890 refusal to join the Scottish League and later amateur seasons fall outside. Kept as decided.

Marking (mar): a dedicated search found nothing on zonal vs man marking for Queen's Park or 1870s-80s Scottish football. The mar axis is covered only formally (via defensive-block and pressing facts about the two-back/two-half-back defence and territorial pressure); the audit should treat zone vs man as unknown.

Pressing: the only facts are territorial ('hemmed Clydesdale in their own territory', 1875; 'untiring pertinacity', 1876). They show the team pinning opponents back, not a pressing scheme; weigh them lightly for blo.

Shape in club matches 1872-73: Robinson and Wilson et al. describe a 2-2-6 for Scotland (= Queen's Park) on 1872-11-30; the SFHG says Queen's Park reverted to the English 1-2-7 or 2-1-7 after that match and only took up the 2-2-6 for good around 1873 (Scotsman report of 1873-12-13). Sources disagree for late 1872 to 1873.

Passing origin: Wilson et al. (2025) quote The Field (March 1872: 'judicious plan of passing on') and The Graphic (14 Dec 1872: 'adepts in passing the ball'); the SFHG says the 5 March 1872 match shows 'no evidence of ball passing' and the Scotsman's 1872 international report mentions only dribbling. Keep the conflict; do not treat Queen's Park as the inventor of passing.

Wikipedia attributes 'Combination was the chief characteristic of the Queen's Park play' to Robinson (1920); the sentence was not found in the chapters read (I, VIII, IX, XII, XIII, XXIV), so it is not used.

Stated view: there was no manager. The only dated statements by club officials (secretaries' reports of 1874 and 1877, quoted by Robinson from the minutes) are about effort and winning back the cup, not about how to play; they are saved as attributed, so stated-view stays a gap.
1880s tactics (wing play, three half-backs, Blackburn finals) rest almost entirely on Robinson's 1920 club history, partly his own narration; no independent period analysis was read for 1880-89.

sources.title: The Evolution of Football Passing in Nineteenth-Century Britain (Wilson, Stocks, Wood, Clarke; Int. J. History of Sport 42:3)
sources.evidence: Peer-reviewed history quoting The Field (March 1872, fn 75/89) on the Wanderers v Queen's Park FA Cup tie: "the Scotchmen played in such energetic style and followed the ball up so quickly, after the Sheffield fashion, that for the first quarter of an hour they rather surprised their English opponents … Their [Queen's Park] style of play is very much after the fashion of Sheffield, as they dribble little and usually convey the ball by a series of long kicks, combined with a judicious plan of passing on." The authors add: "Terms like 'backed each other up' and 'played well together' seem common around 1872 and 1873 for Queens Park". Read in the PDF text.

sources.title: The Evolution of Football Passing in Nineteenth-Century Britain (Wilson, Stocks, Wood, Clarke; Int. J. History of Sport 42:3)
sources.evidence: On Scotland (all Queen's Park players) v England, 30 Nov 1872, quoting The Graphic (14 Dec 1872) / North British Daily Mail (2 Dec 1872): "The Southrons [English], however, did not play to each other so well as their opponents, who seem to be adepts in passing the ball". Earliest Scottish 'combined' references found by the authors: "a 'combined play' reference to a Queens Park v Glasgow Wanderers game in the Glasgow Herald on the April 7, 1873". Their reading: "early Queens Park and Scottish passing, possibly like early Sheffield passing, was rudimentary which gradually evolved from backing up and close combination play".

sources.title: The Evolution of Football Passing in Nineteenth-Century Britain (Wilson, Stocks, Wood, Clarke; Int. J. History of Sport 42:3)
sources.evidence: C.W. Alcock, The Football Annual 1878 (period writer, fn 29), as quoted: "'Passing on' is different to 'backing-up' ... It has been the combination of dribbling and passing that has made the Queen's Park Eleven such a splendid team." The paper's overall conclusion: "passing was effectively deployed, but not necessarily invented in Scotland."

sources.title: The Evolution of Football Passing in Nineteenth-Century Britain (Wilson, Stocks, Wood, Clarke; Int. J. History of Sport 42:3)
sources.evidence: "The Scottish team, who were substantially smaller in stature and weight, however, worked together in pairs allowing them to support each other and so were able to successfully compete, with the game ending 0 - 0." Also The Field (9 Mar 1872, fn 99) on the Wanderers tie: Queen's Park's "method of driving the ball with the head is precisely the same as that adopted in Sheffield".

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. VIII: The First International
sources.evidence: Club history (1920) drawing on period press. "The Scots were arranged with six forwards, two half-backs, two backs, and the goalkeeper." England: "one goalkeeper, one back, one half-back, and eight forwards." Return match 8 Mar 1873: "The English adopted the Scottish formation in the return International".

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. VIII: The First International
sources.evidence: Period reports quoted by Robinson. Glasgow Herald, 2 Dec 1872: "The home club played well together, and carried the ball down into the enemy's quarters by vigorous rushes". North British Daily Mail, 2 Dec 1872: "Leckie, M'Kinnon, and others dribbling so smartly that the English goal was closely besieged." Herald on physique: England's "average being about two stones heavier than the Scotchmen", with England having "the advantage in pace".

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. VIII: The First International
sources.evidence: "both these International teams were selected solely by the Queen's Park captain, Mr. Gardner." (1872 and 1873 internationals).

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. III: The Pioneers
sources.evidence: "The Queen's Park team for the first thirteen years was under the control of a captain, whose power was absolute"; "He appears to have been sole judge of the merits of a player, and he had also to be thoroughly conversant with the rules." At the meeting of 29 April 1880 the captaincies were deleted from Rule II and team management was handed to a match committee with "power to select teams and arrange matches". Vice-captains (from 1873) "selected teams to play practice and club games against a side chosen by the captain".

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. III: The Pioneers
sources.evidence: Context only, before the period: captain Robert Gardner "was the first to issue a card to the players indicating each man's position on the field" (the Hamilton game, pre-1872). The SFHG passing-game page likewise records Gardner "giving out written instructions prior to matches" before 1872. Shows fixed positions set by the captain, but the event is outside profilePeriod.

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. XII: Three Historic Games
sources.evidence: The match reporter (paper not named) on Queen's Park v Vale of Leven, Scottish Cup, 16 Jan 1875: "The styles of play of the two clubs were widely different." "That of the Queen's Park is much the more scientific, all of their forwards relying upon their skill in dribbling"; by contrast "A good many of the Vale men, notably one of the half-backs, seemed to devote themselves to heavy charging". On Weir: "Weir can keep possession of the ball for a time against any single player in Scotland".

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. XII: Three Historic Games
sources.evidence: Robinson's own narration (no quote marks) of the 30 Dec 1876 Vale of Leven tie: "Dumbartonshire football has ever been different from the close inner dribbling and scientific passing which the Queen's Park had developed, and cultivated since its inception". On that day, in a quagmire: "The Queen's Park did not play nearly so well together as their opponents". Author's retrospective characterisation, not a period quote.

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. XII: Three Historic Games
sources.evidence: Territorial pressure, not a described pressing scheme. Herald on the Scottish Cup semi-final v Clydesdale (March 1875): Queen's Park "at once hemmed Clydesdale in their own territory, speedily securing a goal". North British Daily Mail on Wanderers v Queen's Park, Oval, 5 Feb 1876: "The Englishmen had to work very hard to resist the untiring pertinacity of the Scots."

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. XXVI: Three Half-Backs
sources.evidence: Two backs, two half-backs, six forwards until late 1886. Three half-backs tried on 18 and 25 April 1885: "The system after these two trials was condemned, and the defence left to Campbell and Gow." After the Renton defeat of 6 Nov 1886 "the Queen's Park immediately after the Renton reverse became a convert to the new practice", "though it did so with manifest reluctance". Veterans' view: "the advantage gained by having two centre forwards to finish up, more than counterbalances any loss".

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. XXVI: Three Half-Backs
sources.evidence: Defence with only four outfield players behind six forwards, relying on two mobile half-backs: "Much depends upon the calibre of the pair of halves." Campbell and Gow "were capable of covering a lot of ground, both being speedy, and with no end of resource." Nothing on how they marked (zone or man).

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. XXVI: Three Half-Backs
sources.evidence: One recorded case of changing shape for an opponent: "It was, however, decided to meet the enemy with his own weapons" for Preston North End's visit to Hampden, 25 Sep 1886 (three half-backs), lost 6-1; "the old arrangement was reverted to" for the Whitefield tie the following Saturday. Against Blackburn Rovers' three halves at Hampden on 19 Sep 1885 Queen's Park kept two and won 7-1, so "the old arrangement was naturally considered the better."

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. XIV: Queen's Park Team in the Making
sources.evidence: "Once the eleven had been evenly balanced the players were retained." "The substitutes were all tried before being given a permanent place in the First Eleven." "Ability alone was the qualification." Older players were, "on emergencies, dragged them out of retirement" (Robinson calls it "scarcely a wise policy"). Also: the three half-back formation was adopted in the Charity Cup final v Rangers, 13 May 1880, "according to the 'Scottish Football Annual'".

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. XV: Recruiting
sources.evidence: "the club relied solely on its own resources for almost the first ten years"; "It was an axiom with the club that no player was to be solicited, or pressed to join". On youth vs experience: "Whether was it better to maintain the strength of the team by men of reputation and experience" ... "The Queen's Park chose the better part." "Its own junior players did not always receive promotion—a standing grievance with the youngsters". From 1876 it took established players from Third Lanark, Caledonian, Ayr Thistle and (1884) Rangers.

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. XV: Recruiting
sources.evidence: Rule passed at the adjourned AGM, 9 April 1873: "That no members play against the club except by consent of the captain, and must play for the club when wanted"; the club "even went the length of removing from the roll, the names of players who did not respond to the usual circular".

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. XIX: Queen's Park and the English Cup
sources.evidence: 1885 FA Cup semi-final replay at Derby: "Watt and Harrower, in the centre, kept the wings liberally supplied, passing and dribbling most brilliantly." "Sellar, playing on the left wing-Watt going centre-excelled himself." In the 1885 final, forced forward changes "led to an absence of combination, and the resultant slackness near goal." Robinson's narration, period not quoted.

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. XIX: Queen's Park and the English Cup
sources.evidence: 1884 FA Cup run: "The Olympic could do nothing against the splendid back play of the Scots." v Aston Villa: "the magnificent back play of the Queen's Park, than whom there are not a better four in the world." 1885 final: "Arnott did the work of two at back." Before a 1885 tie "fault had been found with the Queen's Park players for lack of condition."

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. XXIV: Queen's Park and International Games
sources.evidence: Early 1880s: E. Fraser and W. Anderson, "the greatest combination of right-wing players ever seen"; "the Fraser-Anderson combination was the observed of all observers" (1883); J. L. Kay "a left-wing forward whose fame will never die". 'Combination' here means a paired wing partnership. Robinson's narration.

sources.title: History of the Queen's Park Football Club 1867–1917 (Richard Robinson), ch. X: Early Honorary Secretaries' Reports
sources.evidence: Match secretary Morton on 1886-87: "only twice in that season had the same team been put on the field" (thirty-eight players used), blamed for the poor season.

sources.title: The Passing-Game
sources.evidence: Counter-reading (SFHG, undated, no author). The 5 March 1872 match "contains no evidence of ball passing"; the Scotsman's report of the November 1872 international "makes no mention of passing or combination by the Scottish team", quoting it as "The Scotch now came away with a great rush, Leckie and others dribbling the ball so smartly". The page credits the passing game to the Vale of Leven, "seemingly more fully still from specifically Renton".

sources.title: The Scots Game's First Team?
sources.evidence: Queen's Park's third home match at the first Hampden, 13 Dec 1873, won 2-0 (opponent not recorded here): the Scotsman's "report of the match has Queen's Park taking the field as two full-backs, two half-backs and six forwards, a 2-2-6." The page argues that after Nov 1872 Queen's Park "had reverted to playing the English, the failing English 1-2-7 or 2-1-7, but now seen the error of its ways."

sources.title: Formation Evolution
sources.evidence: Glasgow Herald, 15 Mar 1873 (on Glasgow football generally): "the beautiful dribbling game is beginning to be appreciated in Glasgow." The page says that around 1873 "even Queen's Park had had to come around" to the 2-2-6 already used by Vale of Leven, Renton and Dumbarton.

sources.title: The "Combination" Game (Iain Campbell Whittle)
sources.evidence: On Scotland (Queen's Park) 30 Nov 1872: "It was a Box-Four, two full-backs and two half-back, in front of the goalkeeper and captain, Robert Gardner", "behind just six forwards, a 2-2-6"; "Effective expansion of the Box-Four in attack and contraction in defence required direction from the captain". On club games: "Perhaps its internal games were played thus but there is no proof."

sources.title: Golden Era (Iain Campbell Whittle)
sources.evidence: c.1880: "2:3:5 was gaining ground, even being tried by Queen's Park." Watson "would be tried at proto-centre-half behind a single centre-forward and two wing-pairings"; then "Queen's Park would revert to 2:2:6".

sources.title: The tale of Queen's Park: the early innovators who became last of the amateurs
sources.evidence: "Scotland went 2-2-6 while England fielded a more attacking 1-1-8." Reliability caveat: the same article gives the March 1872 Wanderers tie as a 5-0 win with "the Queen's Park men dribbling and passing, while their opponents indulged chiefly in heavy kicking"; the tie was 0-0, so that passage is not used.

statedView.quote: The popularity of the game we love is due in no small measure to the energy and pluck of this club.
the members will exercise such diligence in the coming season as will ensure a recapture of that trophy

influences.note: Queen's Park is an exemplar of the combination game; The Field (1872) already saw its play as 'after the fashion of Sheffield'.

confidence.reason: Period press quotes for 1872-76 reach us through a peer-reviewed history (Wilson et al. 2025) and Robinson's 1920 club history; 1880s tactics rest mostly on Robinson's own narration. Sources disagree on whether Queen's Park passed in 1872 and on its club formation in 1872-73. No evidence at all on marking, transitions or set pieces, and no stated view (no manager).
